What makes the grapevine so fascinating?

The grapevine, which ripens into heavy hanging bunches, is a fascinating plant that grows by climbing along a vine. Since it can't stand on its own, it grips tightly onto something and climbs up.

We've gathered all kinds of stories about the grapevine — grapevine facts, grape tendrils, and grapevine ecology.

content.text:
Nature and science facts about the grapevine

The grapevine is a climbing plant that can't stand on its own, so its tendrils coil in spirals and grip firmly onto a support. Flowers bloom in May and June, and once pollinated, grapes form and ripen from August to October. The antioxidants in the grape skin (such as anthocyanins) protect the fruit from pests and ultraviolet rays, and some grapevines live for hundreds of years while still bearing fruit.

Great things to observe together

Point out details like the tendrils (spiraling and gripping), the bunches (many grapes), the skin color (antioxidants), and the seasonal changes. It's a great idea to talk together about, "How does a grape grow upward?"

Parent guide — extending into observation and hands-on activities

Look at a bunch of grapes together, count how many there are, and observe the color of the skin. Watch a photo or video of tendrils coiling around something, and try mimicking "coiling and gripping" with a piece of string.

content.text:
Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)

Q. How does a grapevine grow upward?
A. Its tendrils coil in spirals and grip firmly onto a support to climb. It can't stand up on its own.

Q. Why does grape skin have color?
A. It contains antioxidants like anthocyanins, which protect the fruit from pests and ultraviolet rays.

Q. How can we observe this at home?
A. Try counting the grapes in a bunch, observing the skin color, and mimicking a tendril "coiling and gripping" with a string.
